title: Linux Basics
summary: What Linux is, how the shell works, and the anatomy of a command.

sections.p: When you open a terminal you are talking to a program called a shell (usually Bash). You type a command, press Enter, the shell runs it and prints the result. Everything you will learn here - from copying files to administering servers - happens through this simple loop.
sections.code:
whoami
date
echo "I am learning Linux"

sections.p: Commands follow a pattern: the program name, then options (flags that change behavior, like -l), then arguments (what to act on). Options usually start with a dash; long versions start with two.
sections.code:
ls -l /etc
#  │  │   └── argument: what to list
#  │  └────── option: long format
#  └───────── the command itself

sections.p: You never need to memorize everything. man opens the manual for any command, and history shows what you have typed before. Inside a manual page, press q to quit and / to search.
sections.code:
man ls
history 5

tasks: Show your last 5 commands with history 5

title: Navigation
summary: Move confidently around the filesystem with pwd, ls and cd.

sections.p: The filesystem is one big tree that starts at / (the root). You are always 'in' one directory - the working directory. pwd prints it, ls shows what's around you, and cd moves you.
sections.code:
pwd
ls
ls -la

sections.p: An absolute path starts with / and works from anywhere (/var/log). A relative path starts from where you are (logs/app.log). Two special names help: . is the current directory and .. is the parent.
sections.code:
cd /etc          # absolute
cd ..            # up one level
cd -             # back to where you were

sections.p: Every user has a home directory (yours is /home/student in this trainer). The shortcut ~ means home, and cd with no arguments always takes you there.
sections.code:
cd
pwd
ls ~

title: Working with Files
summary: Create, view, copy, move and delete files - safely.

sections.p: touch creates an empty file (or updates its timestamp). cat prints a file's contents; head and tail show just the beginning or end, which matters for long files like logs.
sections.code:
touch notes.txt
echo "first line" > notes.txt
cat notes.txt

sections.p: cp copies, mv moves - and because renaming is just moving to a new name, mv is also the rename command. Both silently overwrite existing destinations, so add -i when unsure.
sections.code:
cp notes.txt backup.txt
mv backup.txt archive.txt
ls

sections.p: rm deletes permanently. There is no trash bin on the command line. Before any rm with a wildcard, run ls with the same pattern first to preview exactly what will match.
sections.code:
ls *.txt      # preview
rm archive.txt

tasks: Write a line into it with echo and >

title: Directories

sections.p: mkdir creates directories. Its -p flag creates whole nested paths in one go and never complains if part already exists - which makes it the safe default in scripts.
sections.code:
mkdir projects
mkdir -p projects/2026/august
tree projects

sections.p: Directories need cp -r to copy (r for recursive). rmdir removes only empty directories - a built-in safety net. For non-empty ones you need rm -r, which deserves a moment of double-checking every time.
sections.code:
cp -r projects projects-backup
rmdir empty-dir
rm -r projects-backup

title: Permissions
summary: Read, write, execute - who can do what, and how to change it.

sections.p: ls -l shows ten characters like -rwxr-xr--. The first is the type (- file, d directory). Then three triplets: owner, group, others - each with read (r), write (w) and execute (x) bits.
sections.code:
ls -l /etc/passwd
# -rw-r--r-- 1 root root ...
# owner: read+write · group: read · others: read

sections.p: Symbolic mode reads like a sentence: chmod u+x adds execute for the user (owner). Octal mode sets everything at once: r=4, w=2, x=1, summed per triplet - so 755 means rwxr-xr-x.
sections.code:
chmod +x script.sh
chmod 644 notes.txt
ls -l

sections.p: Every file has an owner and a group; chown changes them (root only). sudo runs one command with root privileges - powerful and dangerous in equal measure. Never use chmod 777 as a fix: it hands write access to everyone.
sections.code:
sudo chown student notes.txt
sudo whoami

title: Users & Groups
summary: Accounts, groups and the commands that manage them.

sections.p: whoami tells you who you are; id adds your numeric UID and every group you belong to. Groups exist so permissions can be granted to teams instead of person by person.
sections.code:
whoami
id
groups

sections.p: useradd -m creates a user with a home directory; passwd sets their password. usermod -aG adds them to a group - and the -a (append) matters: -G alone replaces every existing membership.
sections.code:
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash dana
sudo passwd dana
sudo usermod -aG sudo dana

sections.p: who lists logged-in users; w adds what they are running plus the system load. On shared servers these are your situational awareness commands.
sections.code:
who
w

title: Networking
summary: Check connectivity, addresses, DNS and open ports.

sections.p: Debug connectivity in layers: ping your gateway (LAN works?), ping a public IP like 8.8.8.8 (internet works?), then ping a domain name (DNS works?). Where the chain breaks tells you what to fix.
sections.code:
ping -c 3 192.168.1.1
ping -c 3 8.8.8.8
ping -c 3 example.com

sections.p: ip is the modern tool for interfaces and routing. ip addr shows your IP addresses; ip route reveals the default gateway your traffic leaves through.
sections.code:
ip addr
ip route
hostname -I

sections.p: Every network service occupies a port. ss -tulpn lists listening TCP/UDP sockets and the processes behind them - the definitive answer to 'is my server actually running, and on which port?'.
sections.code:
ss -tulpn
curl -I https://example.com

tasks: Show your IP addresses with ip addr

title: Processes
summary: See what's running, understand load, and stop things cleanly.

sections.p: ps aux is a snapshot of every process with its owner, CPU and memory. top is the live version, refreshing continuously - press q to leave it.
sections.code:
ps aux
top

sections.p: kill sends signals by PID. The default SIGTERM asks a process to exit and lets it clean up; SIGKILL (-9) is the un-ignorable sledgehammer. Try polite first: data-losing crashes often trace back to a hasty kill -9.
sections.code:
pgrep -l nginx
kill 812
kill -9 812   # last resort

sections.p: Append & to run a command in the background. jobs lists them; fg brings one forward, Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground task and bg resumes it in the background.
sections.code:
sleep 300 &
jobs
kill %1

tasks: List all processes with ps aux
Find a process by name with pgrep

title: Services & systemd
summary: Start, stop, enable and debug system services.

sections.p: Long-running programs (web servers, databases) run as services managed by systemd. systemctl start|stop|restart changes their state now; status shows whether they are healthy, their PID and their latest log lines.
sections.code:
systemctl status ssh
sudo systemctl restart ssh

sections.p: start affects only the current boot. enable makes a service launch at every boot. They are independent - forgetting enable is why 'it worked until we rebooted'. enable --now does both at once.
sections.code:
sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
systemctl is-enabled nginx

sections.p: journalctl is the systemd log reader. Filter by unit with -u, follow live with -f, and constrain by time with --since. It replaces hunting through /var/log for many services.
sections.code:
journalctl -u nginx --since today
journalctl -f

tasks: Show the status of the ssh service

title: System Administration
summary: Disk space, memory, packages, scheduled jobs and shutdowns.

sections.p: Three commands answer 'how is this machine doing?': df -h (disk space per filesystem), free -h (memory - read the 'available' column, not 'free'), and uptime (load averages).
sections.code:
df -h
free -h
uptime

sections.p: On Debian/Ubuntu, apt manages packages. The two-step rhythm matters: apt update refreshes the catalog, apt install fetches the software. On RHEL-family systems the same rhythm uses dnf.
sections.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install htop

sections.p: crontab -e edits your scheduled jobs. Five fields - minute, hour, day-of-month, month, weekday - then the command. Cron's environment is minimal, so always use absolute paths in the command.
sections.code:
crontab -l
# 0 2 * * * /home/student/backup.sh  → 02:00 daily

title: Security Essentials
summary: SSH keys, firewalls, checksums and safe habits.

sections.p: SSH key pairs replace passwords with cryptography: the private key stays on your machine, the public key goes on the server. ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates a modern pair; ssh-copy-id installs it remotely.
sections.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id student@server
ssh student@server

sections.p: A firewall drops traffic to ports you haven't opened. With ufw, the golden rule on a remote machine is: allow SSH first, enable second - the reverse order locks you out mid-session.
sections.code:
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status

sections.p: Checksums prove a download arrived intact and unmodified. Compare sha256sum output against the value published by the project. And audit logins: last shows history, lastlog shows each account's most recent entry.
sections.code:
sha256sum ubuntu.iso
last -n 5

tasks: Allow port 22 and check ufw status

title: Shell Scripting
summary: Variables, pipes, redirection and your first scripts.

sections.p: The pipe | feeds one command's output into the next - small tools composing into big answers. > writes output to a file (overwriting), >> appends, and 2> captures error output separately.
sections.code:
ps aux | grep nginx
sort names.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn > report.txt

sections.p: NAME=value sets a shell variable; export makes it visible to programs you launch. Double quotes expand variables, single quotes do not - the source of a thousand script bugs.
sections.code:
GREETING="hello"
echo "$GREETING world"
export EDITOR=nano

sections.p: A script is commands in a file, starting with a shebang line telling Linux which interpreter runs it. Make it executable with chmod +x, then run it with ./name. Add set -euo pipefail near the top so failures stop the script instead of compounding.
sections.code:
echo '#!/bin/bash' > hi.sh
echo 'echo "hi from a script"' >> hi.sh
chmod +x hi.sh
./hi.sh

tasks: Build a pipeline with ps aux | grep

title: Advanced Linux
summary: find, awk, sed, tar and the power-tool patterns of daily admin work.

sections.p: find searches live by name, size, age and type - then acts on the results. The safety pattern: run it with just the tests first, review the list, and only then add -exec or -delete.
sections.code:
find /var/log -name '*.log' -size +50M
find . -type f -mtime -1
find /tmp -name '*.tmp' -delete

sections.p: grep finds lines, sed transforms them, awk computes over fields. Together they turn raw logs and config files into answers. Learn one pattern from each and expand as needed.
sections.code:
grep -c ERROR app.log
sed -i.bak 's/DEBUG=true/DEBUG=false/' app.conf
awk -F: '{print $1}' /etc/passwd

sections.p: tar czf creates compressed archives, tar xzf extracts them (mnemonic: Create/eXtract Zip File). rsync -avz synchronizes trees efficiently, locally or over SSH - and rsync -n dry-runs any risky sync first.
sections.code:
tar czf backup.tar.gz project/
tar xzf backup.tar.gz -C /tmp
rsync -avzn src/ dst/   # dry run
